parts.name: Epineurium
parts.description: Epineurium: the dense irregular connective tissue that binds the fascicles into a nerve - a tough outer coat plus looser interfascicular epineurium between the fascicles, carrying fat and the vasa nervorum. It can be half the cross-section of a large nerve, cushions the fascicles against compression, and is the layer sutured in an epineurial nerve repair. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Epineurial collagen bundles
parts.description: Collagen bundles of the outer epineurium: type I collagen running mostly along the nerve, gently crimped, so a nerve can lengthen a few per cent as a joint moves before its fascicles are loaded. Beyond roughly 8–10 % stretch the intraneural blood flow and conduction fail. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Perineurium
parts.description: Perineurium: concentric lamellae of flattened perineurial cells (each layer with a basal lamina on both sides, joined by tight junctions) with thin collagen between them. It wraps every fascicle, gives it tensile strength, and with the endoneurial capillaries forms the blood–nerve barrier. Fascicles divide and merge along a nerve, so their number changes from level to level; a perineurial repair sutures fascicle to fascicle. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Endoneurium
parts.description: Endoneurium: loose connective tissue (fine collagen, fibroblasts, a few mast cells and macrophages) between the individual nerve fibres inside a fascicle, bathed in endoneurial fluid. After an axon is cut, its endoneurial tube with the Schwann cells inside (bands of Büngner) guides regrowth at about 1–3 mm per day - which is why axonotmesis recovers and neurotmesis needs repair. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Myelin sheaths (internodes)
parts.description: Myelin sheaths (internodes): each internode is the compacted spiral membrane of one Schwann cell - in the CNS one oligodendrocyte myelinates many axons. Myelin (P0, PMP22, MBP) insulates the axon so the impulse jumps from node to node. In life internodes are ~100 times the fibre diameter (0.2–1.5 mm); here they are drawn far shorter so several nodes fit in the block. In section each myelinated fibre is a pale ring round a central axon. Attacked in Guillain–Barré syndrome and CIDP; PMP22 duplication causes Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 1A. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Axons
parts.description: Myelinated axons: the conducting processes of motor neurons, large sensory neurons (Aα/Aβ) and Aδ pain and temperature fibres, 1–20 µm across; the axon is about 60–70 % of the fibre diameter (g-ratio). Conduction velocity rises with diameter, up to about 120 m/s. Cut axons degenerate distally (Wallerian degeneration). Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Nodes of Ranvier
parts.description: Nodes of Ranvier: ~1 µm gaps between successive Schwann cells where the axon is bare and packed with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (Nav1.6), with K⁺ channels hidden under the paranodal myelin. The action potential is regenerated only here - saltatory conduction. Antibodies to nodal gangliosides (GM1) cause the acute motor axonal form of Guillain–Barré. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Schwann cell nuclei
parts.description: Schwann cell nuclei: one elongated nucleus per internode, in the thin collar of cytoplasm outside the myelin; the Remak Schwann cells have their own. Schwann cells come from the neural crest and give rise to schwannomas (bilateral vestibular schwannomas in neurofibromatosis type 2). Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Remak Schwann cells
parts.description: Remak (non-myelinating) Schwann cells: each holds a bundle of several thin axons, every one sunk in its own trough of Schwann cell cytoplasm with no myelin - a Remak bundle. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Unmyelinated axons (C fibres)
parts.description: Unmyelinated axons (C fibres): 0.2–1.5 µm, conducting at 0.5–2 m/s - slow burning pain, temperature, itch and postganglionic sympathetic fibres. They outnumber the myelinated fibres in most cutaneous nerves and are lost early in small-fibre neuropathy (diabetes, amyloid). Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Endoneurial capillaries
parts.description: Endoneurial capillaries: continuous, non-fenestrated capillaries whose tight junctions form the vascular half of the blood–nerve barrier. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale. These are disconnected longitudinal representative segments, not an authored arteriole-to-venule network; neutral capillary colour has no flow gradient.

parts.name: Schwann cell outer cytoplasm
parts.description: Thin Schwann-cell layer, exaggerated schematically for teaching. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Schwann basal lamina
parts.description: Thin Schwann-cell layer, exaggerated schematically for teaching. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Epineurial fat
parts.description: Epineurial fat: lobules of adipocytes in the interfascicular epineurium that cushion the fascicles. Nerves with little fat and a superficial course (ulnar at the elbow, common fibular at the fibular neck) are the ones most prone to compression palsy. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Vasa nervorum (arterioles)
parts.description: Vasa nervorum (arterioles): a longitudinal anastomosing plexus in the epineurium, fed segmentally by nearby arteries, whose branches pierce the perineurium obliquely to supply the endoneurial capillaries. Their occlusion in diabetes or vasculitis causes ischaemic mononeuropathy and mononeuritis multiplex (e.g. a painful third-nerve palsy that spares the pupil). Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.

parts.name: Vasa nervorum (venules)
parts.description: Vasa nervorum (venules): epineurial veins draining the endoneurial capillaries back through the perineurium. Their oblique course through it is easily pinched when endoneurial pressure rises - one reason compression neuropathies (carpal tunnel) become ischaemic. Representative teaching sample: three fascicles and enlarged fibres; not a literal nerve census or clinical fibre scale.
